```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, NullFormatter

plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 11, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

DATA = Path("data")
if not DATA.is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Missing data/ folder. Put the project CSV files in data/ beside this QMD before rendering.")
YEAR = 2022
N_TOP = 5

# Conflict-affected or closed economies with highly uncertain estimates.
# Left out of the trend line and the ranking, shown as hollow markers.
EXCLUDE = ["Central African Republic", "North Korea", "Syria", "Palestine"]

ORANGE, BLUE, GREY = "#d95f02", "#1f4e79", "#b0b0b0"


def read_owid(file, value_name, countries_only=True):
    """Our World in Data CSVs: Entity, Code, Year, <value>. Keep the first four columns."""
    df = pd.read_csv(DATA / file).iloc[:, :4]
    df.columns = ["country", "code", "year", value_name]
    if countries_only:
        df = df[df["code"].notna() & ~df["code"].astype(str).str.startswith("OWID")]
    return df


def label_point(ax, text, xy, offset, colour=ORANGE, size=10):
    """Label a point with a short leader line that starts at the edge of the text, not through it.
    offset = (dx, dy) in points from the point to the centre of the label."""
    dx, dy = offset
    ax.annotate(text, xy, xytext=offset, textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                va="bottom" if dy >= 0 else "top", color=colour, fontweight="bold", fontsize=size,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=colour, lw=1,
                                relpos=(0.5, 0.0) if dy >= 0 else (0.5, 1.0), shrinkA=2, shrinkB=4))


def md_table(df):
    """Small helper that prints a data frame as a Markdown table."""
    header = "| " + " | ".join(df.columns) + " |"
    rule = "|" + "|".join(["---"] * len(df.columns)) + "|"
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in r) + " |" for r in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    return "\n".join([header, rule] + rows)


def difference_from_income(df, value_col, gdp_col="gdp_pc"):
    """Value minus the value expected for the country's income (straight-line fit on log GDP).
    Used for shares and years, where a ratio makes less sense. 0 = typical for income."""
    b, a = np.polyfit(np.log10(df[gdp_col]), df[value_col], 1)
    return df[value_col] - (a + b * np.log10(df[gdp_col]))


def relative_to_income(df, value_col, gdp_col="gdp_pc"):
    """Ratio of a country's value to the value expected for its income (log-log fit).
    1.0 = same as countries with similar income; 0.5 = half; 2.0 = double."""
    b, a = np.polyfit(np.log10(df[gdp_col]), np.log10(df[value_col]), 1)
    return df[value_col] / 10 ** (a + b * np.log10(df[gdp_col]))
```

```{python}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false
# ---- Life expectancy and GDP per capita (2022 only; nothing is carried forward) ----
life_all = read_owid("life-expectancy.csv", "life_exp", countries_only=False)
life = read_owid("life-expectancy.csv", "life_exp")
gdp = read_owid("gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv", "gdp_pc")

d = life[life["year"] == YEAR].merge(gdp[gdp["year"] == YEAR], on=["country", "code", "year"])
d = d[d["gdp_pc"] > 0].dropna(subset=["life_exp", "gdp_pc"])

# ---- Income-based benchmark: life expectancy ~ log10(GDP per capita) ----
fit = d[~d["country"].isin(EXCLUDE)].copy()
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log10(fit["gdp_pc"]), fit["life_exp"], 1)
fit["expected"] = intercept + slope * np.log10(fit["gdp_pc"])
fit["gap"] = fit["life_exp"] - fit["expected"]  # actual minus expected
r2 = 1 - ((fit["life_exp"] - fit["expected"]) ** 2).sum() / ((fit["life_exp"] - fit["life_exp"].mean()) ** 2).sum()

top = fit.nlargest(N_TOP, "gap").copy()
excluded_shown = d[d["country"].isin(EXCLUDE) & (d["country"] != "Central African Republic")]

# ---- Health spending per person (PPP), relative to income peers ----
hx = read_owid("annual-healthcare-expenditure-per-capita.csv", "hx")
s = fit.merge(hx[hx["year"] == YEAR][["country", "hx"]], on="country").dropna(subset=["hx"])
s = s[s["hx"] > 0].copy()
s["hx_ratio"] = relative_to_income(s, "hx")
corr_hx = np.corrcoef(s["gap"], np.log10(s["hx_ratio"]))[0, 1]

# ---- Child mortality (% of newborns dying before age 5), relative to income peers ----
cm = read_owid("child-mortality.csv", "cm")
c = fit.merge(cm[cm["year"] == YEAR][["country", "cm"]], on="country").dropna(subset=["cm"])
c = c[c["cm"] > 0].copy()
c["cm_ratio"] = relative_to_income(c, "cm")
corr_cm = np.corrcoef(c["gap"], np.log10(c["cm_ratio"]))[0, 1]

# ---- Income inequality (Gini), latest survey in 2017-2022 ----
gini = read_owid("gini-coefficient.csv", "gini")
g = (gini[(gini["year"] >= 2017) & (gini["year"] <= 2022)]
     .sort_values("year").groupby("country").tail(1)[["country", "gini"]])
q = fit.merge(g, on="country")
corr_gini = np.corrcoef(q["gap"], q["gini"])[0, 1]

# ---- Sanitation: share of people using at least basic sanitation, 2022 ----
# The download is named "...-faciltities.csv" (Our World in Data's spelling) or "...-facilities.csv";
# find it whichever way it is spelled.
san_files = sorted(DATA.glob("share-of-population-with-improved-sanitation*.csv"))
if not san_files:
    raise FileNotFoundError("Put the sanitation CSV (share-of-population-with-improved-sanitation-...csv) in the data/ folder.")
san = read_owid(san_files[0].name, "san")
sn = fit.merge(san[san["year"] == YEAR][["country", "san"]], on="country").dropna(subset=["san"]).copy()
sn["san_diff"] = difference_from_income(sn, "san")
corr_san = np.corrcoef(sn["gap"], sn["san_diff"])[0, 1]

# ---- Schooling: average years, latest available year (2020; partly projected) ----
SCHOOL_YEAR = 2020
sch = read_owid("mean-years-of-schooling-long-run.csv", "sch")
sc = fit.merge(sch[sch["year"] == SCHOOL_YEAR][["country", "sch"]], on="country").dropna(subset=["sch"]).copy()
sc["sch_diff"] = difference_from_income(sc, "sch")
corr_sch = np.corrcoef(sc["gap"], sc["sch_diff"])[0, 1]

# Sanity checks: stop early if the fitted sample cannot support the story.
assert len(fit) >= N_TOP, "Not enough countries for a top-five ranking."
assert fit["country"].is_unique, "Duplicate countries in fitted 2022 sample."
assert np.isfinite(fit[["life_exp", "gdp_pc", "expected", "gap"]].to_numpy()).all(), "Non-finite model values."

five = top["country"].tolist()
five_text = ", ".join(five[:-1]) + " and " + five[-1]
gap_lo, gap_hi = top["gap"].min(), top["gap"].max()
```

# The short version

*Wealth matters for how long people live, but it does not settle it.* Across the world, richer countries tend to live longer. Yet some countries live noticeably longer than their income would suggest. This story looks at the five that do so by the widest margin in 2022, and asks what might help explain it.

```{python}
#| label: summary
#| output: asis
print(f"""
- **Income explains a lot, but not everything.** Across {len(fit)} countries, income alone accounts for about {r2:.0%} of the differences in life expectancy.
- **Five countries beat the odds.** {five_text} live roughly {gap_lo:.0f} to {gap_hi:.0f} years longer than their income would predict.
- **There is no single route.** Health spending relative to income varies widely among the five, and lower child mortality and better sanitation than expected fit some of them but not all.
- **These are associations, not proof of cause.** Our data shows patterns that are worth investigating, not what made them happen.
""")
```

# 1. The big picture: do richer countries live longer?

Life expectancy has risen in every region of the world since 1950. The gap between regions has narrowed, but it has not closed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-regions
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy by world region, 1950–2023. Source: Our World in Data (UN World Population Prospects)."
regions = {"Europe": "#4c6a9c", "Oceania": "#8c8c8c", "Americas": "#c8553d",
           "Asia": "#2a9d8f", "World": "#1b4d1b", "Africa": "#a64ca6"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.4))
for name, colour in regions.items():
    sub = life_all[(life_all["country"] == name) & (life_all["year"] >= 1950)]
    ax.plot(sub["year"], sub["life_exp"], color=colour, lw=3 if name == "World" else 2)
    if name == "Oceania":      # same end value as Europe, so share one label
        continue
    label = "Europe / Oceania" if name == "Europe" else name
    ax.text(sub["year"].max() + 1, sub["life_exp"].iloc[-1], label, color=colour,
            fontweight="bold", va="center", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(1950, 2040)
ax.set_xticks(range(1950, 2030, 10))
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy at birth (years)")
ax.grid(axis="y", ls="--", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: regions-text
#| output: asis
def region_value(name, year):
    return float(life_all[(life_all["country"] == name) & (life_all["year"] == year)]["life_exp"].iloc[0])

gap1950 = region_value("Europe", 1950) - region_value("Africa", 1950)
gap2023 = region_value("Europe", 2023) - region_value("Africa", 2023)
print(f"In 1950, people in Europe lived about {gap1950:.0f} years longer than people in Africa. "
      f"By 2023 that gap had narrowed to about {gap2023:.0f} years, but it remains large.")
```

## At the same income, lives can still differ a lot

Before we look for patterns, a puzzle. Take countries with almost the same income, between 4,000 and 6,000 international dollars per person.

```{python}
#| label: fig-same-income
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy of countries with a GDP per capita of 4,000 to 6,000 international dollars, 2022. Each dot is one country."
band = fit[(fit["gdp_pc"] >= 4000) & (fit["gdp_pc"] <= 6000)]
lo, hi = band["life_exp"].min(), band["life_exp"].max()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5.2))
others = band[band["country"] != "Nicaragua"]
ax.scatter(others["gdp_pc"], others["life_exp"], s=80, color=GREY, edgecolor="white", zorder=2)
nic = band[band["country"] == "Nicaragua"].iloc[0]
ax.scatter(nic["gdp_pc"], nic["life_exp"], s=140, color=ORANGE, edgecolor="#222", zorder=3)
ax.annotate(f"Nicaragua ({nic['life_exp']:.1f})", (nic["gdp_pc"], nic["life_exp"]), xytext=(-90, 6),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="center", color=ORANGE, fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)
ax.annotate("", xy=(6150, lo), xytext=(6150, hi), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#444", lw=1.3))
ax.text(6230, (lo + hi) / 2, f"About {hi - lo:.0f} years\napart at almost the\nsame income", va="center", fontsize=11, color="#444")
ax.set_xlim(3800, 7200)
ax.set_ylim(50, 80)
ax.set_xlabel("GDP per capita (international dollars, 2011 prices)")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy at birth (years)")
ax.grid(axis="y", ls="--", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: same-income-text
#| output: asis
print(f"Among these {len(band)} countries, life expectancy ranges from {lo:.0f} to {hi:.0f} years. "
      f"Nicaragua is at the top of the group. Income clearly matters, but it cannot be the whole story.")
```

Does money explain the differences? To find out, we compare each country's life expectancy with its income per person in 2022. Income is shown on a logarithmic scale, which means each step to the right is a tenfold increase.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy and GDP per capita, 2022. The blue line is the income-based expectation. Hollow markers are countries left out of the trend because their data is highly uncertain."
x_line = np.logspace(np.log10(d["gdp_pc"].min() * 0.9), np.log10(d["gdp_pc"].max() * 1.1), 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(fit["gdp_pc"], fit["life_exp"], s=28, color=GREY, alpha=0.85, lw=0)
ax.scatter(excluded_shown["gdp_pc"], excluded_shown["life_exp"], s=34, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#9a9a9a")
ax.plot(x_line, intercept + slope * np.log10(x_line), color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(45, 90)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,.0f}"))
ax.set_xlabel("GDP per capita (international dollars, 2011 prices, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy at birth (years)")
ax.grid(axis="y", ls="--", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: scatter-text
#| output: asis
print(f"The pattern is clear: richer countries tend to live longer, with diminishing returns at high incomes. "
      f"Income alone accounts for about {r2:.0%} of the differences between the {len(fit)} countries in our trend. "
      f"That leaves a lot unexplained, and some countries sit well above the line.")
```

# 2. The surprise: five countries beat the odds

We call the distance between a country's actual life expectancy and the value expected for its income the **gap**. A positive gap means people live longer than income alone would predict. Here are the five countries with the largest positive gaps in 2022.

```{python}
#| label: fig-top
#| fig-cap: "The five countries furthest above the income trend, 2022. Labels show the gap in years."
offsets = {"Cuba": (-60, 34), "Lebanon": (45, 40), "Cape Verde": (70, -42),
           "Nicaragua": (-110, 22), "Bangladesh": (-90, -40)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(fit["gdp_pc"], fit["life_exp"], s=28, color=GREY, alpha=0.85, lw=0)
ax.scatter(excluded_shown["gdp_pc"], excluded_shown["life_exp"], s=34, facecolors="none", edgecolors="#9a9a9a")
ax.plot(x_line, intercept + slope * np.log10(x_line), color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax.scatter(top["gdp_pc"], top["life_exp"], s=90, color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
for _, r in top.iterrows():
    label_point(ax, f"{r['country']} (+{r['gap']:.1f})", (r["gdp_pc"], r["life_exp"]),
                offsets.get(r["country"], (0, 30)))
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(45, 90)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,.0f}"))
ax.set_xlabel("GDP per capita (international dollars, 2011 prices, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy at birth (years)")
ax.grid(axis="y", ls="--", alpha=0.3)
ax.text(0.99, 0.03, f"{len(fit)} countries. Blue line: life expectancy expected for each income.\n"
        "Orange: the five countries furthest above it. Hollow: left out (data very uncertain).",
        transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color="#444",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec="#ddd"))
plt.show()
```

## How rare is it?

```{python}
#| label: fig-waffle
#| fig-cap: "Each square is one country in 2022, ordered from the largest gap above the income trend."
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
LIGHT_ORANGE = "#f2b27a"
g = fit.sort_values("gap", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
n_c, cols = len(g), 14
n_rows = int(np.ceil(n_c / cols))
n_big = int((g["gap"] >= 5).sum())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 5.2))
for i in range(n_c):
    rr, cc = divmod(i, cols)
    colour = ORANGE if i < 5 else (LIGHT_ORANGE if i < n_big else GREY)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((cc, n_rows - 1 - rr), 0.86, 0.86, color=colour))
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, cols + 8.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.3, n_rows + 0.2)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
near = g.loc[5:n_big - 1, "country"].tolist()
lx = cols + 0.7
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lx, n_rows - 2.0), 0.6, 0.6, color=ORANGE))
ax.text(lx + 1.0, n_rows - 1.7, f"Our five: {g.loc[4, 'gap']:.1f} to {g.loc[0, 'gap']:.1f}\nyears above expected", va="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lx, n_rows - 4.2), 0.6, 0.6, color=LIGHT_ORANGE))
ax.text(lx + 1.0, n_rows - 3.9, f"{' and '.join(near)}: almost\ntied with the fifth", va="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lx, n_rows - 6.4), 0.6, 0.6, color=GREY))
ax.text(lx + 1.0, n_rows - 6.1, f"All other countries ({n_c - n_big})", va="center", fontsize=10.5)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: waffle-text
#| output: asis
print(f"Only {n_big} of {n_c} countries ({n_big / n_c:.0%}) live five or more years longer than their income predicts. "
      f"Our five are the ones with the largest gaps, but {' and '.join(near)} are almost tied with the fifth, "
      f"so the five are good examples rather than a sharply separate group.")
```

## How fast did they improve?

```{python}
#| label: fig-change
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy in 2000 and 2022 for the five countries and the typical country (median start value and median gain)."
l0 = life[life["year"] == 2000][["country", "life_exp"]].rename(columns={"life_exp": "y0"})
l1 = life[life["year"] == 2022][["country", "life_exp"]].rename(columns={"life_exp": "y1"})
sl = fit[["country"]].merge(l0, on="country").merge(l1, on="country")
sl["chg"] = sl["y1"] - sl["y0"]
typ_start, typ_chg = sl["y0"].median(), sl["chg"].median()
five_rows = sl[sl["country"].isin(five)].set_index("country").loc[five]


def spread(vals, gap):
    """Nudge label positions apart so they do not overlap."""
    vals = np.array(vals, float)
    order = np.argsort(vals)
    out = vals.copy()
    for k in range(1, len(order)):
        if out[order[k]] - out[order[k - 1]] < gap:
            out[order[k]] = out[order[k - 1]] + gap
    return out


names = five + ["Typical country"]
y0s = list(five_rows["y0"]) + [typ_start]
y1s = list(five_rows["y1"]) + [typ_start + typ_chg]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.6))
for nm, a0, a1 in zip(names, y0s, y1s):
    typ = nm == "Typical country"
    ax.plot([0, 1], [a0, a1], color="#777" if typ else ORANGE, lw=2.2, ls="--" if typ else "-", marker="o", ms=6)
for nm, a0, a1, lp, rp in zip(names, y0s, y1s, spread(y0s, 1.15), spread(y1s, 1.15)):
    typ = nm == "Typical country"
    ax.text(-0.03, lp, f"{nm}  {a0:.1f}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10.5, color="#555" if typ else "#222",
            fontweight="normal" if typ else "bold")
    ax.text(1.03, rp, f"{nm}  {a1:.1f}  (+{a1 - a0:.1f})", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=10.5,
            color="#555" if typ else "#222", fontweight="normal" if typ else "bold")
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 1.75)
ax.set_ylim(58, 83)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1])
ax.set_xticklabels(["2000", "2022"], fontsize=12)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: change-text
#| output: asis
bang = five_rows.loc["Bangladesh"]
print(f"Since 2000, the typical country gained about {typ_chg:.0f} years of life expectancy. Bangladesh gained "
      f"{bang['chg']:.0f}, while Cuba, which started high, gained only {five_rows.loc['Cuba', 'chg']:.1f}. "
      f"The five countries did not all travel the same road to their current position.")
```

# 3. Beyond income: what else might matter?

## Health spending: more than one route

If money buys health, countries that beat the odds might simply spend more on health care. We compare each country's health spending per person with what countries at a similar income spend (a value of 1.0 means typical for that income).

```{python}
#| label: fig-spending
#| fig-cap: "Health spending per person relative to countries with similar incomes, 2022 (log scale; 1x = typical for income). Labels show each country's life expectancy gap."
t = s[s["country"].isin(five)].sort_values("hx_ratio")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
colours = [ORANGE if r >= 1 else "#7570b3" for r in t["hx_ratio"]]
ax.barh(t["country"], t["hx_ratio"] - 1, left=1, color=colours, height=0.55)
ax.axvline(1, color="#333", lw=1.2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.3, 18)
ax.set_xticks([0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 4])
ax.set_xticklabels(["0.3x", "0.5x", "1x", "2x", "4x"])
ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(NullFormatter())
for i, (_, r) in enumerate(t.iterrows()):
    ax.text(max(r["hx_ratio"], 1) * 1.1, i, f"{r['hx_ratio']:.1f}x   (gap +{r['gap']:.1f} yrs)", va="center", fontsize=10)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
ax.grid(axis="x", ls="--", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: spending-text
#| output: asis
lo = t.iloc[0]; hi = t.iloc[-1]
print(f"{hi['country']} spends about {hi['hx_ratio']:.1f} times what its income peers spend, while "
      f"{lo['country']} spends about {lo['hx_ratio']:.1f} times as much. Across {len(s)} countries, "
      f"spending relative to income is moderately associated with the gap (correlation {corr_hx:.2f}), "
      f"so spending seems to be part of the story, but not the whole story. "
      f"Spending also says little about how well the money is used, and the estimate for {hi['country']} is uncertain.")
```

## Child survival: part of the explanation

Deaths of young children pull down average life expectancy, so countries where fewer children die than their income would predict tend to show a positive gap.

```{python}
#| label: fig-child
#| fig-cap: "Child mortality relative to countries with similar incomes (horizontal axis, log scale; below 1x means lower than expected) and the life expectancy gap (vertical axis), 2022."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.8))
ax.axhline(0, color="#333", lw=1)
ax.axvline(1, color="#999", lw=1, ls="--")
ax.scatter(c["cm_ratio"], c["gap"], s=28, color=GREY, alpha=0.85, lw=0)
h = c[c["country"].isin(five)]
ax.scatter(h["cm_ratio"], h["gap"], s=90, color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
label_offsets = {"Cuba": (-50, 26), "Nicaragua": (10, 50), "Cape Verde": (-70, -40),
                 "Lebanon": (-15, 50), "Bangladesh": (55, 32)}
for _, r in h.iterrows():
    label_point(ax, r["country"], (r["cm_ratio"], r["gap"]), label_offsets.get(r["country"], (0, 30)))
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4])
ax.set_xticklabels(["0.25x", "0.5x", "1x", "2x", "4x"])
ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(NullFormatter())
ax.set_xlabel("Child mortality relative to income peers (below 1x = fewer child deaths than expected)")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy gap (years)")
ax.grid(ls="--", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: child-text
#| output: asis
lower = h[h["cm_ratio"] < 0.8]["country"].tolist()
typical = h[h["cm_ratio"] >= 0.8]["country"].tolist()
print(f"Across {len(c)} countries, lower-than-expected child mortality goes together with a larger gap "
      f"(correlation {corr_cm:.2f}). Among our five, {', '.join(lower)} have clearly fewer child deaths than their income predicts, "
      f"while {' and '.join(typical)} are about typical. So early-life survival may help explain some of the five, "
      f"but not all. Because child deaths lower life expectancy directly, part of this link is built into how life expectancy is calculated.")
```

## Inequality: little to add

```{python}
#| label: gini-text

have = [x for x in five if x in q["country"].values]
print(f"Income inequality (the Gini index) has only a very weak link to the gap (correlation {corr_gini:.2f} across {len(q)} countries). "
      f"Recent survey data is also missing for most of our five; only {' and '.join(have)} have a value for 2017–2022.")
```

## Sanitation: a clearer link

Safe sanitation keeps disease from spreading. Here we compare the share of people using at least basic sanitation with what is typical for each country's income.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sanitation
#| fig-cap: "Sanitation relative to countries with similar incomes (horizontal axis, percentage points; right of zero = better than expected) and the life expectancy gap (vertical axis), 2022."
def diff_chart(df, xcol, xlabel, offsets):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.8))
    ax.axhline(0, color="#333", lw=1)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#999", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.scatter(df[xcol], df["gap"], s=28, color=GREY, alpha=0.85, lw=0)
    hh = df[df["country"].isin(five)]
    ax.scatter(hh[xcol], hh["gap"], s=90, color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
    for _, r in hh.iterrows():
        label_point(ax, r["country"], (r[xcol], r["gap"]), offsets.get(r["country"], (0, 30)))
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy gap (years)")
    ax.grid(ls="--", alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

diff_chart(sn, "san_diff", "Sanitation relative to income peers (percentage points; above 0 = better than expected)",
           {"Cuba": (-45, 36), "Lebanon": (50, 36), "Cape Verde": (-20, -42), "Bangladesh": (0, 42)})
```

```{python}
#| label: sanitation-text
#| output: asis
sn5 = sn[sn["country"].isin(five)]
better = sn5[sn5["san_diff"] > 5]["country"].tolist()
typical_s = sn5[sn5["san_diff"] <= 5]["country"].tolist()
missing_s = [x for x in five if x not in sn["country"].values]
verb = "is" if len(typical_s) == 1 else "are"
txt = (f"Across {len(sn)} countries, better-than-expected sanitation goes together with a larger gap "
       f"(correlation {corr_san:.2f}), a clearer link than we found for income inequality. "
       f"{', '.join(better)} have much better sanitation than their income predicts, "
       f"while {' and '.join(typical_s)} {verb} about typical.")
if missing_s:
    txt += f" {' and '.join(missing_s)} is not in the sanitation data."
print(txt)
```

```{python}
diff_chart(sc, "sch_diff", "Years of schooling relative to income peers (years; above 0 = more than expected)",
           {"Cuba": (45, 36), "Nicaragua": (10, 46), "Bangladesh": (-65, 36)})
```

```{python}
#| label: schooling-text
#| output: asis
missing_c = [x for x in five if x not in sc["country"].values]
sc5 = sc[sc["country"].isin(five)].copy()
above = sc5.loc[sc5["sch_diff"] > 1, "country"].tolist()
near_s = sc5.loc[sc5["sch_diff"].between(-1, 1), "country"].tolist()
below = sc5.loc[sc5["sch_diff"] < -1, "country"].tolist()
parts = []
if above:
    parts.append("more schooling than their income predicts: " + ", ".join(above))
if near_s:
    parts.append("approximately typical schooling: " + ", ".join(near_s))
if below:
    parts.append("less schooling than their income predicts: " + ", ".join(below))
if missing_c:
    parts.append("no schooling data: " + ", ".join(missing_c))
print(f"Across {len(sc)} countries, years of schooling relative to income has only a weak link to the gap "
      f"(correlation {corr_sch:.2f}). "
      + ("Among the five, " + "; ".join(parts) + ". " if parts else "")
      + "Schooling figures for 2015 onwards are projections, so this comparison requires caution.")
```

# What this means

Money matters, but it is not the whole story. Countries with very different incomes and health budgets can still live longer than expected, and they get there by different routes. These countries do not prove that a particular policy works. They are good starting points for asking what else is going on.

# How we did it

- **Data:** Our World in Data, year 2022 only (nothing carried forward from earlier years). Life expectancy comes from UN World Population Prospects, GDP per capita from the Maddison Project Database 2023, health spending per person (PPP) from the WHO via the World Bank, child mortality from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, the Gini index from the World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, sanitation from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, and average years of schooling from Barro and Lee (the 2020 values are partly projections).
- **Expected life expectancy:** a straight-line trend of life expectancy against the logarithm of GDP per capita. "Predicts" in our title means this fitted estimate, not a forecast of the future. A country's gap is its actual life expectancy minus the expected value.
- **Relative to income:** for spending and child mortality, we compare each country with the value typical for its income, using the same kind of trend on a log scale.

```{python}
#| label: sample-text
#| output: asis
print(f"**Sample.** {len(d)} countries have both life expectancy and income in 2022. We left out "
      f"Central African Republic, North Korea, Syria and Palestine because conflict or closed economies make their "
      f"estimates highly uncertain, so the trend uses {len(fit)} countries. With them included, the trend would explain "
      f"less, and North Korea, Syria and Palestine would appear among the largest gaps.")
```

## Limits

- The main income-based model is cross-sectional (2022), so it cannot establish changes over time or causation. The separate historical charts describe trends but do not change that limitation.
- All results are associations, not causes.
- Income is measured per person and adjusted for living costs, but both income and spending are estimates, especially for lower-income countries.
- Spending per person says nothing about the quality or reach of health care.
- Five countries are illustrations. The patterns are tested across all countries with data.
